transcript:
This message comes from Kachava. A little boost goes a long way, especially when it comes to caring for your gut during the holiday season and beyond.
Introducing Kachava's new 3-in-1 digestive boost. Simply mix in to your favorite Kachava shake or any cold beverage.
Go to Kachava.com and use code NPR for 15% off your first order. That's K-A-C-H-A-V-A.com. Code NPR.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston. A leaked intelligence memo says the Pentagon is putting new limits on military
cooperation with Canada. The Canadian Defense Minister says the two militaries are still working closely together.
Julian Abraham reports from Halifax. The leaked classified Department of Defense memo first reported by the Washington Post has dominated
conversations at the Halifax International Security Forum.
Republican South Dakota Senator Mike Rounds confirmed its existence in a speech at the forum. While it was a classified discussion,
it was one that was put together several months ago, only recently signed, and then it was unfortunately then released publicly.
Rounds says, according to the memo, U.S. military officials will need permission to attend Canadian think tank events or social gatherings.
The latest strain on an already fraught relationship between the two allies.
But speaking at the forum, Canada's Defense Minister David McGinty insisted cooperation with the U.S. on defense, security, and intelligence
continues. For NPR News, I'm Julian Abraham in Halifax.
United Nations climate talks are heading into overtime this weekend in Turkey.
NPR's Rachel Waldholz reports negotiations were supposed to wrap up on Friday, but talks have spilled into a second night.
Some countries, they want to come away from this climate summit with an agreement that explicitly calls on the world to transition
away from fossil fuels.
That's because burning coal and oil and natural gas is the primary driver of global warming, and they want that called out.
But other countries, especially big oil producers like Saudi Arabia and Russia,
don't want language that specifically targets fossil fuels. And so that has become a big
sticking point for some countries this year. That's NPR's Rachel Waldholz reporting.
Starting January 1st, work requirements are being added to Medicaid, the public health insurance program for low-income people.
NPR's Selena Simmons-Duffin reports health policy experts warn those new rules will increase the number of people who are uninsured.
Right now, Medicaid covers about 70 million low-income Americans.
About 5 million of them are projected to become uninsured because of the new work requirements.
Adriana McIntyre is a health policy professor at Harvard.
She points out enrollment has to shrink in order to achieve savings in the Republican budget law.
You only save money in Medicaid if you are covering fewer people.
And if you're only covering fewer healthy people, you're not saving that much money.
It's covering fewer people who need health care.
That's where you get scare quotes, savings out of work requirements.
Democrats say reversing this policy is a top priority when they take over the majority in Congress.
Selena Simmons-Duffin, NPR News, Washington.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
President Trump says he's ready to work with Democrats in the next Congress to cap credit card interest rates at 10 percent.
Trump pitched the cap during his 2024 campaign. Banks and congressional Republicans showed little interest while Democrats have backed the idea.
The median credit card rate is just over 22 percent.
Researchers estimate a 10 percent cap could save Americans $100 billion a year.
After traveling for more than eight years, a joint European-Japanese mission has gone into orbit around the planet Mercury.
The probe should provide scientists with a wealth of new information about the innermost planet in the solar system.
Joe Palka reports.
Mercury is an intriguing planet.
It has an incredible number of scientific mysteries.
Anne Pomier at the Carnegie Institution is one of the scientists on the Beppe Colombo mission.
She says scientists have found evidence that there is ice at the poles of the planet, odd for a planet so close to the sun.
It also has a larger metal core than expected.
The fact that this planet is shrinking also is another mystery.
Beppe Colombo is scheduled to start answering scientific questions next spring.
But first, it will spend several months adjusting its orbit and checking out its instruments.
For NPR News, I'm Joe Palka.
The latest Grand Theft Auto video game brought in nearly $3.8 billion in sales around the world on its first day.
It's the first new game in the series in 13 years.
The previous installment took three days to reach $1 billion in sales.
This is NPR News.
This message comes from the National Audubon Society.
Want to protect the planet?
For Audubon, it all begins with birds.
Their work protecting birds and habitats for over a century has helped bring back species like the bald eagle.
Now they need you to tackle the threats birds face today.
Because when birds thrive, so does the planet.
Become a member by December 31st to get the spring issue of their quarterly magazine.
Give today at Audubon.org/NPR.

topics.text: Pentagon limits military cooperation with Canada, per leaked classified memo; Canada says ties continue
UN climate talks in Turkey run into overtime as fossil fuel transition language stalls
Medicaid work requirements take effect January 1, expected to leave about 5 million uninsured
Trump says he will work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10 percent
Joint European-Japanese BepiColombo probe enters orbit around Mercury after eight-year journey
Grand Theft Auto game earns nearly $3.8 billion in sales on its first day
